overview: Two Gram-positive cocci from normal gut flora and among the most common causes of hospital-acquired infection, distinguished mainly by prevalence and resistance patterns.
genZNote: Same genus, but E. faecium brought the vancomycin resistance to the party more often.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The most commonly isolated Enterococcus species in clinical infections, part of normal gastrointestinal flora.
aspects.valueB: The second most common Enterococcus species clinically, notable for higher rates of antibiotic resistance.

aspects.label: Clinical Frequency
aspects.valueA: Accounts for the majority of enterococcal infections overall (urinary tract infections, endocarditis, bacteremia).
aspects.valueB: Less frequent overall, but disproportionately represented among vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE) isolates.

aspects.label: Antibiotic Resistance Pattern
aspects.valueA: Generally more susceptible to ampicillin and vancomycin than E. faecium.
aspects.valueB: More frequently intrinsically resistant to ampicillin and more likely to acquire vancomycin resistance (VRE).

aspects.label: Clinical Relevance
aspects.valueA: Common cause of urinary tract infections, biliary infections, and subacute bacterial endocarditis.
aspects.valueB: Increasingly important cause of hospital-acquired, multidrug-resistant infections, especially in immunocompromised patients.

aspects.label: Identification
aspects.valueA: Grows on bile-esculin agar, hydrolyzing esculin; catalase-negative, grows in 6.5% NaCl.
aspects.valueB: Also grows on bile-esculin agar and 6.5% NaCl; species-level distinction typically requires biochemical panels or molecular methods.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: More common overall; generally more antibiotic-susceptible.
aspects.valueB: Less common overall, but higher rate of vancomycin/ampicillin resistance.
